en: A Mirror for the Chan School: Caoxi, by Tuīyǐn.
There is a thing here that, from the very beginning, has been luminous and spiritually alert; it has never been born and never perished. Its name is...
It cannot be described; it cannot be grasped.
What is this "one thing"? An ancient master sang: "Before the ancient Buddhas were born, there was a single, perfectly complete form.
Even Śākyamuni did not comprehend it; how could Kāśyapa have transmitted it? This is why this one thing has never been born.
"It has never been extinguished; this is called 'not being able to obtain its form or its name. The Sixth Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying, "I have a thing that has no name and no character;
do you all recognize it? Master Shenhui immediately stepped forward and said, "It is the source of all Buddhas;
it is the Buddha-nature of Shenhui. This is why he was known as the "illegitimate son" of the Sixth Patriarch. Huairang—
The Chan Master came from Mount Song. The Sixth Patriarch asked him, "What thing comes like this? The Master was at a loss for words.
It was not until the eighth year that he finally accepted it himself, saying, "To describe it as a single thing is immediately off the mark.
This is why he is considered the legitimate son of the Sixth Patriarch. The sages of the Three Teachings emerge from this very phrase. Who is there to raise it? How regrettable!
"Seizing the eyebrows.
When Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world, they stir up waves where there is no wind.
"Buddhas and patriarchs" refers to the World-Honored One, Kāśyapa. "Appearing in the world" means taking great compassion as their essence to deliver sentient beings.
Yet, when one observes from the perspective of a single reality, the face and countenance of every person are fundamentally perfected;
how could they require others to apply rouge or powder? This is why the world-transcending [path] gives rise to waves of realization.
The *Gaganagañja Sūtra* states: "Words and letters are demonic activities; names and signs are demonic activities; even the words of the Buddha are demonic activities."

This is the intended meaning. This directly presents the fundamental state: where Buddhas and Patriarchs have no functional power, heaven and earth lose their luster, and the sun and moon are without light.
Nevertheless, the Dharma has many meanings and people have many capacities; thus, it is not an impediment to making provisional arrangements.
The Dharma is a single reality; humans are sentient beings. The Dharma possesses the principle of being unchanging while following conditions;
humans possess the capacity for sudden awakening and gradual cultivation. Therefore, there is no hindrance to the establishment of written words and verbal expressions.

This is what is meant by "the public office does not admit a needle, yet private access allows for carriages and horses. Although sentient beings are said to be perfectly accomplished, they are still born...
Lacking the eye of wisdom, one willingly undergoes the cycle of rebirth; therefore, were it not for the golden lancet that transcends the world, who could scrape away the thick film of ignorance?
As for those who cross the ocean of suffering to ascend to the shore of bliss, all is due to the grace of Great Compassion.
Thus, even a life as vast as the sands of the Ganges cannot repay even a ten-thousandth part of this kindness. This extensively illustrates the response to new conditioning.
The profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is such that when the King ascends the jeweled throne, the rustic elder breaks into song.
One may forcibly establish various names—whether "mind," "Buddha," or "sentient beings"—but one must not cling to these names to give rise to conceptual understanding.
The very essence is it; to stir a thought is to deviate from it.
To forcibly establish three names for a single reality is the teaching’s necessity;
not to cling to these names and give rise to conceptual interpretations is likewise the necessity of Chan. Raising and pressing, establishing and destroying—these are all [the same].

The Dharma King is one who possesses mastery over the Dharma. This [verse] concludes the preceding section and introduces the following: the affairs and essential natures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are each distinct.
It is like encountering a timely rain after a long drought, or meeting an old friend in a foreign land.

The transmission of the mind through three stages by the World-Honored One constitutes the essential meaning of Chan; that which was taught throughout his entire life constitutes the gateway of the teachings. Therefore it is said:
"Chan is the Buddha’s mind; the teachings are the Buddha’s words."
As for the "three locations": first, sharing half his seat before the Many-Sons Stūpa; second, holding up a flower at the assembly on Vulture Peak;
and third, manifesting his two feet within the coffin beneath the twin trees. These are what are known as the "separate transmission of Kāśyapa" and the "lamp of Chan.
As for the "one lifetime," it refers to the five teachings expounded during the forty-nine years [of his ministry]. The first is the Teaching for Humans and Devas.
First is the Hīnayāna teaching; second is the Mahāyāna teaching; third is the Sudden teaching;
fourth is the Perfect teaching—this is what is meant by the so-called "Ocean of Teachings" transmitted by Ānanda. Thus, the source of Chan and the teachings is the World-Honored One;
the branches of Chan and the teachings are Kāśyapa and Ānanda. Through wordlessness, one arrives at the ultimate.
That which is beyond words is Chan; that which uses words to reach the wordless is the teaching. Thus, while the mind is the essence of Chan, speech is the method of instruction.
Although the Dharma is of a single flavor, the gap between their respective insights is as vast as heaven and earth.
This distinguishes between the two paths of Chan and the Teachings (Dharma). One must not let this pass by;
to lie prostrate amidst the weeds is to miss the point. Therefore, if one loses it in words, then even the plucking of the flower and the smile are merely traces of the Teachings.
If one attains it in the mind, then even the coarse and subtle speech of the world are the Chan principles of the Special Transmission Outside the Teachings.
Because the Dharma has no name, words cannot reach it. Because the Dharma has no form, the mind cannot reach it.

To attempt to express it with the mouth is to lose the fundamental King of the Mind. Once the fundamental King of the Mind is lost, then the World-Honored One’s holding up of the flower and Kāśyapa’s smile are entirely reduced to stale words;
in the end, they are nothing at all. To attain it within the mind is not merely a matter of verbal display.
He skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma; even the warbling of a swallow can be a profound discourse on the true nature (*dharmatā*).
This is why Master Baoji rejoiced in body and mind upon hearing the sound of weeping, and why Master Baoshou saw his face and eyes opened wide when struck by a fist.
This clarifies the relative depth of Chan and the teachings. It is like holding a bright pearl in one’s hand, playing with it back and forth.
I have a single word: sever all deliberation and forget all conditions; sit in a state of utter non-action. When spring comes, the grass grows green of its own accord.
"Severing deliberation and forgetting conditions" means attaining this within the mind; such is what is called the person of the leisurely Way. Alas!
As for such a person, they are fundamentally without conditions and fundamentally without affairs. When hungry, they eat; when weary, they sleep.
Ambling at will among green waters and blue mountains; sleeping in peace and ease at fishing villages and wine shops.

One knows nothing of the years or the sexagenary cycle; when spring comes, the grass remains as green as ever. For those who wish to turn their light back upon themselves for even a single thought after this parting:
It was thought that there was no one [to receive this], yet fortunately there is this one person.
In the Teaching School (Jiaomen), only the Dharma of the One Mind is transmitted; in the Chan School, only the Dharma of Seeing Nature (jianxing) is transmitted.
The mind is like the substance of a mirror, while nature is like the light of the mirror. Nature is inherently pure; it is immediately restored in its suchness.
One attains the original mind. This secret and weighty attainment of the meaning lies in a single thought-moment. Layer upon layer of mountains and waters—this is the pure and white ancestral style.
Commentary: There are two kinds of mind: first, the mind of the fundamental source; second, the mind that grasps at signs through ignorance. As for its nature...
There are two kinds: first, the fundamental nature of phenomena (dharmatā); second, the nature of the relative correspondence between essence and characteristics.

Therefore, practitioners of Chan and the doctrinal schools alike are deluded, clinging to names to produce understanding; they may mistake the shallow for the profound, or the profound for the shallow, which consequently becomes a great sickness in their contemplative practice. Thus, this is clarified here.
However, when the Buddhas preach the sutras, they first analyze all phenomena and subsequently teach ultimate emptiness.
When the Patriarchs reveal their phrases, the traces are severed from the realm of thought, and the principle is manifested at the source of the mind.
The Buddhas serve as the reliance for ten thousand generations; therefore, it is necessary to reveal the principle exhaustively. The Patriarchs, while in this very moment, bring about liberation;
thus, they cause the "intention" (yi) to penetrate the profound. "Trace" (ji) refers to the traces of the Patriarchs' words; "intention" (yi) refers to the mental ground of the student.
To point and indicate haphazardly is like trying to bend one's arm outward when it cannot be bent that way.
The Buddhas speak of the bow; the Patriarchs speak of the string. Only when the Buddhas teach the dharma of non-obstruction does one return to the single flavor.
Only by brushing away the traces of this single flavor does the "one mind" shown by the Patriarchs manifest. Therefore, it is called the "story of the cypress tree in the courtyard."

That which has never before existed in the Dragon Canon (Nāgārjuna’s collection) is here described as the bow being curved and the string being straight. The "Dragon Canon" refers to the scriptures stored in the Dragon Palace.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhaozhou replied, "The cypress tree in the courtyard. This is what [is meant here].
This refers to the essence of Chan that transcends the teachings. "When the fish swims, the water is turbid; when the bird flies, feathers fall.
Therefore, students first use the words of the teachings as they truly are to discern the two meanings of the unchanging following conditions (*bùbiàn suíyuán*).

These are the nature and characteristics of one's own mind. The two gates of sudden awakening and gradual cultivation constitute the beginning and end of one's own practice. Only after this should one set aside the teachings.
Regarding the meaning: simply take the present moment of one's own mind and investigate the essence of Chan; then you will surely attain something.
This is what is called "finding a living path beyond the body.
While those of superior faculties and great wisdom are not limited by this, those of middling or inferior faculties must not attempt to leap over the stages. This is the doctrinal meaning.

This is the principle of the unchanging following conditions. While sudden enlightenment and gradual cultivation involve a sequence of before and after, in the Dharma of Chan, within a single thought-moment, the unchanging follows conditions;
essence and appearance, substance and function, are fundamentally simultaneous. It is neither identical nor different, yet it is both identical and non-identical.
Therefore, the Master, relying on the Dharma, points directly beyond words: in a single thought-moment, one sees one's nature and becomes a Buddha. Let go.
This is the meaning of the teaching. When it is clearly manifest, the clouds are hidden in the deep valley; where it is profoundly dense, the sun shines upon the clear sky.
Generally, a student must investigate the "live word" (huoju) and not the "dead word" (siju).
If you can realize it beneath the "live word," you are fit to serve as a teacher to the Buddhas and Patriarchs; if you realize it beneath the "dead word," you will not even be able to save yourself.
Hereafter, I specifically cite live words to enable you to awaken and enter [the Way]. To see Linji, one must be an iron man.
The commentary states: The *huatou* (critical phrase) has two aspects: the gate of the sentence (*ju*) and the gate of the meaning (*yi*).
To investigate the sentence is the direct and decisive gate, the "live word" (*huo ju*), because it leaves no path for the mind and no path for speech, being beyond all grasp.

To investigate the meaning is the gate of the perfect and sudden, the "dead word" (*si ju*), because it possesses a rational path and a verbal path, involving the characteristics of hearing, understanding, and reflection.
In all cases of the public cases (gong'an) for fundamental investigation, apply yourself with total dedication to the practice.

Be like a hen brooding her eggs, like a cat stalking a mouse, like one hungry thinking of food, like one thirsty thinking of water, or like a child yearning for its mother; then there will surely come a time of thorough penetration.

The ancestral masters' *kōans* number one thousand seven hundred cases, such as "The dog has no Buddha-nature," "The cypress tree in the courtyard," "Three pounds of flax," and "A dried-up shit-stick.
A hen brooding her eggs is the continuous succession of warm breath;
a cat pouncing on a mouse is the unmoving eye-mind. As for hunger, one thinks of food; when thirsty, one thinks of water.
To remember one's mother arises entirely from a sincere heart, not from a contrived mind; therefore, it is called "urgent.
If one lacks this sense of urgency in the practice of Chan meditation, there is no possibility of attaining thorough penetration.
Practicing Chan requires three essentials: first, a great root of faith; second, a great spirit of indignation; and third, a great state of doubt.
If even one of these is lacking, it is like a tripod with broken legs; it will ultimately become a useless vessel.
The Buddha said: "For one who attains Buddhahood, faith is the root. Yongjia said: "One who cultivates the Way must first establish their resolve. Monsan said:
"For one who studies Chan, failing to doubt the words and phrases is a great illness. He further said:
"Beneath great doubt, there will surely be great awakening."
In daily life, whenever you encounter conditions, simply bring up the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature.
As you bring it up again and again, and as doubt arises again and again, you will find that there is no rational path, no logical way, and no flavor to it.
When your mind becomes feverish and stifled with frustration, that is precisely where you let go of body and life; it is also the very foundation for becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor.
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have Buddha-nature or not? Zhaozhou said, "No.

This single character is a pivotal barrier of the Chan school; it is also the weapon for crushing all manner of evil cognitions and perceptions, the very countenance of the Buddhas, and the marrow of the Patriarchs.
One must penetrate this barrier before one can [attain] Buddhahood.
The Patriarch may be anticipated. An ancient eulogy says: "Zhaozhou’s blade is bare; its cold frost and radiant flames blaze.
Should you hesitate to ask 'How is it?', your body will be split in two."
Do not attempt to grasp the "head-word" at the point where it cannot be raised; do not engage in calculation or deliberation.

Furthermore, do not wait for awakening by means of delusion, nor deliberate upon that which is beyond deliberation. When the mind has nowhere to go—like a rat entering a cow’s horn—you will see the sudden severance of the root.
Moreover, that which is habitually calculated and arranged is merely the realm of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which follows along with birth and death.
The bottom of the current is consciousness; the state of terror and panic is consciousness. People today do not recognize this as a sickness;
they merely continue to bob up and down within it.
There are ten kinds of illnesses regarding the *huatou* (the critical phrase): 1. Speculating with the faculty of thought; 2.
Grasping at the core within the movement of raising eyebrows or blinking eyes; 3. Making a living on the path of words; 4. Citing evidence from written texts; 5.

Taking responsibility for the very moment it is raised; 6. Casting it away into the casket of "nothingness"; 7. Interpreting it in terms of existence or non-existence; 8. Interpreting it as being truly non-existent.

To apply rational analysis is to remain lost while waiting for enlightenment. To be free from these ten kinds of maladies, simply shake up your spirit at the moment the story is presented and wonder only: "What is this?"
This matter is like a mosquito on an iron ox; one no longer questions how or what.
Where there is no place to set the beak, one abandons life and plunges in with the whole body.

I reiterate the aforementioned intent so that those who engage with the "live word" shall not falter or retreat. As the ancients said: "In practicing Chan, one must penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs;
in attaining wondrous enlightenment, one must exhaust the path of the mind."
The method of practice is like the art of tuning strings: one must find the balance between tension and relaxation. To be overly diligent leads to attachment; to be forgetful leads to ignorance.
One must remain alert and vivid, yet maintain a subtle, continuous, and pervasive presence.
The lute player said: "Only when the slow and the fast attain the middle way will the pure tones be universal.

The practice of cultivation is also like this: if one is too hurried, it agitates the blood-bags; if one is forgetful, one enters the ghost-cave. When neither slow nor fast, the wondrousness lies within."
When one reaches this stage of cultivation, one is unaware of walking while walking and unaware of sitting while sitting.

At such a time, the eighty-four thousand demonic armies wait at the gates of the six sense organs, manifesting according to the arising of the mind. If the mind does not arise, what can they do? What can they possibly do?
"Māra" is the name for a ghost who delights in birth and death. The eighty-four thousand māra armies are none other than the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings.
Māra originally has no seed; it is those who lose mindfulness during practice who cause its source to branch out.
Sentient beings follow along with their objects, and thus they follow him; practitioners oppose their objects, and thus they oppose him. Therefore—
It is said that when the Way is lofty, demonic influences flourish. Within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one may sometimes see a filial son cutting his own thigh, or see a piglet by its snout;
these are also visions arising from one's own mind that evoke external demons. If the mind does not give rise to them, they do not appear.
Thus, all manner of skillful means are turned into cutting water or blowing upon light. An ancient said: "When the wind moves through a crack in the wall, the demon invades the crack of the mind.
To give rise to the mind is the celestial demon; not to give rise to the mind is the aggregate demon; whether arising or not arising is the affliction demon.
However, within my True Dharma, such matters have never existed from the beginning.

Generally speaking, the forgetting of mental activity is the Buddha-way, while discrimination is the realm of Māra. Yet, what need is there to labor over discerning or disputing the dream-like affairs of the realm of Māra?
If one's practice reaches the point of being a single, unified whole, then even if one cannot achieve penetration in this life, at the moment the light of the eyes falls to the ground,
one will not be led astray by evil karma.
The practitioner is ignorance; Chan is Prajñā. That light and darkness do not oppose one another is a matter of course.

Generally speaking, does the Chan practitioner still recognize the profound depth of the four debts of gratitude? Does he still recognize that this foul body of the four elements decays moment by moment?
Does he still recognize that human life hangs by a thread? Has he, since birth, encountered the Buddhas and Patriarchs? And having heard...

Do you give rise to a sense of wonder toward the Unsurpassed Dharma? Do you maintain your integrity without leaving the Sangha hall? Do you refrain from idle chatter with those in neighboring quarters?
Most importantly, do you strictly avoid fanning the flames of right and wrong? Is the *huatou* clear and unclouded throughout the twelve periods of the day?
When conversing with others, is there no interruption? When seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, do you unify them into a single whole?
When looking back at yourself, do you capture and defeat the Buddhas and Patriarchs? In this life, will you certainly continue the Buddha’s wisdom-life?
When rising or sitting for convenience, do you still contemplate the suffering of hell? Will this retribution-body surely escape saṃsāra? When encountering the eight winds...
"Are the objects and the mind unmoving? This is the principle for practitioners of Chan to examine during their daily activities.
As the ancients said: "If this body is not saved in this present life, what other life shall one wait for to save it?"
The four debts of gratitude are those owed to parents, sovereigns, teachers, and benefactors. Regarding this foul body composed of the four great elements:

a single drop of the father’s semen and a single drop of the mother’s blood possess the moisture of the water element. That the semen becomes bone and the blood becomes skin possesses the solidity of the earth element.
That the mass of semen and blood does not rot or decay possesses the warmth of the fire element.
Furthermore, the nostrils first form as a conduit for the inhalation and exhalation of breath, which is the movement of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
Ānanda said: "The desire for vital energy is coarse, turbid, and foul-smelling; through its mingling, this is what constitutes the ugly body.

That every thought-moment decays and withers means that the light upon the head does not stop for even a single *kṣaṇa*. The face naturally wrinkles and the hair naturally turns white. As it is said, 'Now that it is no longer...'"
"As it was in the past, so shall it not be in the future; this is the nature of impermanence (*anityatā*). Yet, the ghost of impermanence takes killing as its sport;
it is truly fearsome at every moment of thought. Exhalation is the fire of the breath going out; inhalation is the wind of the breath coming in.
The life of a person is entrusted solely to these incoming and outgoing breaths. As for the eight winds (*aṣṭau vāyavaḥ*), they are the favorable and the adverse."
Second is the realm of the hells. A single day and night in the *niraya* (hell) is equivalent to sixty *kalpas* of human time.
The sufferings of boiling cauldrons, glowing embers, sword-trees, and mountain-blades are such that they cannot be fully described in words.
Human birth is more difficult to obtain than finding a needle in the great ocean; regarding this realm, one should feel compassion and issue a warning.
The commentary states: The Dharma teachings presented above are like a person drinking water—their warmth or coldness is known by themselves. Intelligence cannot overcome karma;
even those with dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā) cannot escape the wheel of suffering. Each must examine their own thoughts and not deceive themselves.

Those who merely mimic the words of the teachings seem to have attained awakening when speaking, yet remain deluded when confronted with actual circumstances; this is what is meant by the discrepancy between words and deeds.
This concludes the point regarding self-deception. When words and deeds are at variance, the distinction between the false and the real can be discerned.
If you wish to confront birth and death, you must achieve this single moment of thought that bursts forth and shatters [all barriers]. Only then will you fully comprehend birth and death.
It is like the sound of a lacquer bucket being shattered; only after the lacquer bucket is broken can one truly confront birth and death.
For the Buddhas practicing the Dharma on the causal ground, this is all there is.
However, once that single thought-moment bursts and shatters, one must then seek out an enlightened master to resolve and discern the True Eye.
This matter is extremely difficult; one must give rise to a sense of shame before it can be attained. The Way is like a great ocean, becoming deeper and deeper as one enters it;
be careful not to consider a small realization sufficient. If, after awakening, one does not meet such a person, then even the supreme flavor of *amṛta* (clarified butter) will turn into poison.
It becomes a poisonous drug. An ancient worthy said: "We value only that your eye be correct; we do not value where you practice.
In the past, Yangshan answered Moshan’s question, saying: "The forty fascicles of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* are all the words of Māra. This...
This is the True Eye of Yangshan. Yangshan further asked about the place of practice. Guishan replied, "It is simply a matter of your eye being correct.
[Yangshan] said, "This is why one first opens the True Eye and only afterwards speaks of practice. Therefore it is said:
"If you wish to cultivate practice, you must first attain sudden enlightenment."
I pray that all practitioners will have deep faith in their own minds.

Neither humbling themselves nor exalting themselves, they should know that this mind is fundamentally equal, originally devoid of the distinction between ordinary and sage. Yet, based on the person, there is delusion and awakening, and thus the categories of ordinary and sage arise.

When one is suddenly awakened by the inspiration of a teacher to realize that one’s true self is no different from the Buddha, this is *sudden* [enlightenment]. This is why one does not humble oneself.
It is as the saying goes: "Originally there is not a single thing. To awaken to this and sever habitual tendencies, thereby transforming the ordinary into the sacred, is the gradual approach.
This is why one does not exalt oneself; it is as the saying goes: "Wipe away the dust diligently at all times. To be humble is the sickness of those who study through teachings;
to be haughty is the sickness of those who study Chan. Those who rely on teachings do not believe that the Chan gate offers a path of awakening and entry.

This is the secret instruction. Those who remain deeply mired in provisional teachings and cling to the distinction between the real and the false do not cultivate meditative practice, but instead count the treasures of others;
thus, they naturally give rise to despondency. Zen practitioners do not believe that the gate of the teachings contains the correct path of cultivation and severance.
Although defiled habits arise, one does not feel shame or remorse; although at the initial stage of the fruits there is much pride regarding the Dharma, one thus speaks with excessive arrogance.
Therefore, those who have attained the meaning and cultivate the mind neither humble themselves nor exalt themselves.
The commentary states: "Neither bowing down nor being haughty" briefly cites the initial mind; when the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, this refers to even a single stage of faith.
When citing the bodhisattvas extensively, the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause, thus referring to all fifty-five stages.
If the deluded mind cultivates the Way, it merely assists ignorance.

If awakening has not yet been thoroughly realized, how can such cultivation be called true? The meaning of awakening and cultivation is like the mutual dependence of oil and light, or the complementary support of eyes and feet.
The essential point of practice is simply to exhaust all mundane sentiments; there is no separate "sage's understanding.
When the illness is exhausted, the medicine is removed, and one returns to being the original person.
There is no need to abandon the mind of sentient beings; it is only necessary not to defile one’s own nature. To seek the "correct Dharma" is itself a delusion.
Both the one who abandons and the one who seeks are defiled.
Severing afflictions is termed the Two Vehicles; the non-arising of afflictions is termed Great Nirvana.
"Severing" implies subject and object; "non-arising" means there is neither subject nor object.
One must maintain an empty mind and reflect upon oneself, believing that the single thought-moment of dependent origination is unborn.
This clarifies the arising of nature alone.
Contemplate clearly how killing, stealing, lust, and falsehood arise from the one mind; they are quiescent in their very place—what need is there to further sever them?
This pair clarifies both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*).
The Sūtra says: "Not giving rise to a single thought is called the eternal severance of ignorance. It also says: "When a thought arises, one immediately awakens;
knowing it is an illusion, one departs from it without employing expedient means. Departing from illusion is awakening itself, and there is no gradual progression."
The mind is the illusionist; the body is the illusory city; the world is the illusory garment; names and forms are illusory food.
As for the arising of thoughts and the speaking of the false as true, there is nothing that is not illusion. Furthermore, the beginningless illusion of ignorance all arises from the awakened mind.
Illusion upon illusion is like flowers in the sky. When illusion ceases, it is called "immovability. Therefore, it is like a dream.
One who seeks a physician for a sore awakens to find no remedy; likewise it is with those who understand illusion:
sentient beings perceive birth-and-death and nirvana within that which is unborn, like perceiving the arising and ceasing of flowers in the sky.
Because the nature is fundamentally unborn, it is unarisen nirvāṇa. Because emptiness is fundamentally without flowers, there is no arising or ceasing.
To perceive birth and death is like perceiving the arising of flowers in the sky; to perceive nirvāṇa is like perceiving the cessation of flowers in the sky.
However, arising is fundamentally without arising, and ceasing is fundamentally without ceasing. One need not scrutinize or interrogate these two views.

Therefore, the *Siksasamuccaya-sutra* states: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is not for the sake of delivering sentient beings; it is solely for the sake of delivering one from the two views of birth-and-death and nirvana."
The Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings into parinirvāṇa; yet, in reality, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva simply regards every thought-moment as a sentient being. To realize that the essence of thought is empty is to deliver sentient beings.
Since mindfulness is empty and quiescent, in reality there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. The above has discussed faith and understanding;
although the principle is realized instantaneously, phenomena are not eliminated instantaneously.
Mañjuśrī realizes the truth of the nature of reality; Samantabhadra clarifies dependent origination. His understanding is like a flash of lightning; his practice is like that of a destitute son.
The following section discusses cultivation and realization:

practicing dhyāna while harboring lust is like steaming sand to make rice; practicing dhyāna while harboring killing is like stuffing one's ears while someone shouts; practicing [dhyāna] while harboring theft...
To practice dhyāna while seeking fulfillment like a leaking cup is to practice dhyāna while harboring delusions; it is like carving excrement into incense.
Even if one possesses great wisdom, it will all become the path of Māra.

This clarifies the three trainings of the outflow-free (anāsrava) as the rules for cultivation. Those of the Hīnayāna take the Dharma they receive as their precepts, which provide a coarse purification.
In its ultimate sense, the Mahāyāna takes the gathering of the mind as its precept.

By subtly severing the root [of transgression], there is no violation of the dharma-precepts through the body, and no violation of the mind-precepts through thought. Sexual misconduct severs purity; killing severs compassion;
stealing severs merit; and lying severs truth. Even if one were to achieve wisdom and attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), if one does not [act accordingly]...
If one cuts off killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra and forever lose the true path to Bodhi.

These four precepts are the root of the hundred precepts; therefore, they are explained separately so that one may not even think of transgressing them. Absence of recollection is called *śīla* (precept); absence of conceptualization is called *samādhi* (concentration);
and absence of delusion is called *prajñā* (wisdom). Furthermore, *śīla* is like catching a thief, *samādhi* is like binding the thief, and *prajñā* is like killing him.
Thieves! Furthermore, when the vessel of precepts is complete and firm, the water of concentration is clear and still, and the moon of wisdom finally appears.

These three trainings are truly the source of all dharmas; therefore, they are specifically elucidated so that no outflows remain. How could there be a Buddha without practice at the assembly on Vulture Peak?
